title: Superquants?
hook: The power is not fancy math. It is the courage to say fifty-six when sixty feels cleaner.
counterintuition: Ibbie assumes numbers make people rigid. Used well, numbers keep doubt honest by showing small differences and small updates instead of fake certainty.
tryThisNow: Open a note, write one forecast you already believe about a probability estimate, add a percent and a check date, then write what would make you move the number down.
keyTakeaway: Use numbers to express uncertainty clearly: choose a probability, make finer distinctions when they matter, and update in proportion to the evidence.

breakdown.fastRead:
At 1:15 p.m., Ibbie changes the risk cell from medium to fifty-six. The label hid the disagreement. The number makes it visible. He wants the clean answer now. The paper in front of him will not give it.

Write the odds where the room can see them. Add the date, the question, and the sign that would make you change your mind. A good number does not kill doubt. It gives doubt a shape.

A forecast gets useful when it can be checked later. Confidence without a receipt is only weather in someone else's voice. Keep the receipt.
breakdown.deepRead:
At 7:40 a.m., Mahir, a ferry planner, weighs a wind update against the morning cancellation odds. The forecast moves from 30 to 38, not from 30 to panic. The easy move is to pick the story that feels whole. The better move is to slow down long enough to ask what the record says before this case arrived.

A number is not a costume for certainty. It is a handle. You can move it when the facts move. You can also leave it alone when the new fact is only loud. Granularity is useful when the extra digit changes a real choice.

Picture Odelia rating grant risks in five-point bins until the bins prove too blunt for real choices. The choice is not between swagger and silence. The choice is between a claim that can learn and a claim that can only defend itself.

Use the smallest clean question you can write. Put a date on it. Start from the outside view, the rate for cases like this one, then adjust for what is truly different here. Stop when you can explain the move in plain words.

A limit stays in view. Some events are too tangled, too far out, or too hidden for a sharp answer. The skill is not pretending fog is glass. The skill is knowing when the glass is only dirty enough to wipe.
breakdown.fullRead:
At 5:23 p.m., Zhen, a lab manager, watches two test-failure rates differ by three points. The small difference matters because the batch size is huge. Everyone at the table can feel the pull of a clean story. It lowers stress. It gives the next meeting a script. It also hides the weak joint in the forecast, the part nobody will remember to test unless someone writes it down now.

Hand the room a sharper question. Do not ask whether the whole future will go well. Ask whether a named event will happen by a named date. Ask what would count as yes. Ask what rate similar cases have shown before. The room may groan, because the work feels smaller. The smaller work is the point. It gives reality a place to answer.

A forecaster earns trust by leaving tracks. The first track is the base rate. Before you explain why this case is special, look at how often cases like it have turned out that way. The second track is the update. If a new fact arrives, move the odds by the strength of that fact, not by the size of the feeling it creates. The third track is the review. When the result lands, save the old number and ask which assumption broke.

At 10:02 a.m., Danya, a soccer analyst, refuses to round every player-risk forecast to a neat ten. Her messy numbers keep the coach from treating unlike risks as the same. This is where the craft starts to feel almost physical. The pen pauses. The number changes from 60 to 55, not from 60 to 10, because the new fact is real but not huge. The team can see the move. Nobody has to pretend the old answer was perfect.

False precision is a costume; honest precision is a tool. It keeps judgment from turning into a costume. A person can sound brave while hiding from the record. A quieter person with dates, odds, and reviews may be doing the harder thing.

The limit matters. Long-range shocks, hidden incentives, and fragile systems can make even careful work miss. A good forecaster does not use that as an excuse to blur every claim. She uses it to sort questions. Some deserve a wide range. Some deserve a backup plan. Some deserve no forecast stronger than a shrug.

Try the move on a live claim today. Take one future sentence you hear at work, at home, or in the news. Cut it into a smaller question. Put a probability on it. Write why you chose that number. Then mark the date when you will look again. The act takes two minutes. The habit changes the room because it makes confidence answerable.

examples.title: Ibbie changes medium to fifty-six percent

planSpec.audience: a risk lead replacing labels with probabilities
planSpec.stakes: whether a security risk label hides real disagreement
planSpec.requiredBeat: she turns a vague label into a probability and date

examples.scenario: Ibbie pinches the bridge of her nose at 1:15 p.m. in the security war room, where the risk dashboard glows green, amber, red. The vendor breach is marked medium. Half the engineers read medium as 30 percent, half as 70. The renewal vote is in forty minutes. Ibbie clicks into the cell and types 56 percent chance of material exposure by June 1. The room goes quiet because the label can no longer do everyone's work.
examples.whatToDo: Replace the label with a dated probability. Ask who would move it up or down and why before the renewal vote.
examples.whyItMatters: Medium hides disagreement. A number makes people argue about evidence, which is the argument the decision actually needs.

examples.title: Mahir moves the ferry odds eight points

planSpec.audience: a ferry planner updating cancellation odds
planSpec.stakes: whether a new wind report causes overreaction
planSpec.requiredBeat: he sizes the update to the strength of the signal

examples.scenario: Mahir holds a damp wind map at 7:40 a.m. in the ferry terminal office, salt water dripping from his jacket cuff. The 9:10 crossing sits at 30 percent cancellation on the dispatch board. A fresh gust report comes in higher, but only at the outer buoy. Passengers are already lining up near the coffee kiosk. Mahir's finger hovers over the board. He has to decide whether the update deserves panic or eight clean points.
examples.whatToDo: Move the cancellation forecast to 38 percent and note the outer-buoy source. Wait for the harbor reading before making a larger change.
examples.whyItMatters: The new signal is real but partial. A modest update keeps the forecast responsive without letting one noisy buoy run the terminal.

examples.title: Odelia quits forcing every grant into five bins

planSpec.audience: a program officer ranking project risks
planSpec.stakes: whether blunt categories treat unlike risks as equal
planSpec.requiredBeat: she moves from coarse bins to probabilities where choices differ

examples.scenario: Before lunch, Odelia had thirty grant proposals sorted into five risk bins, the neat stacks squared on her office rug. At 1:52 p.m., she notices two projects in bin three: one has a 42 percent chance of missing its permit, the other 64 percent. Same bin, different bet. She opens a spreadsheet and writes the probabilities beside the folders. By the board call, the stacks look messier, but the funding order finally makes sense.
examples.whatToDo: Use bins only when they are enough for the choice. When two items in the same bin would lead to different actions, write the probabilities.
examples.whyItMatters: Coarse labels are fast, but they can flatten important differences. Finer numbers help only when they change what you do.

examples.title: Zhen refuses to round away three percentage points

planSpec.audience: a lab manager comparing test-failure rates
planSpec.stakes: whether a small difference matters at scale
planSpec.requiredBeat: she keeps a small percentage difference because volume makes it costly

examples.scenario: Zhen stands by the centrifuge at 5:23 p.m., latex gloves snapped at her wrist, while two failure rates sit on the lab monitor. "Seven and ten are basically the same," the plant manager says. Zhen points through the glass at the pallets waiting for release. "At this batch size, three points is twelve thousand units." The manager looks back at the screen. Zhen has to decide whether to round for peace or keep the awkward precision.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the exact rates and translate the difference into units. Let the scale decide whether the extra precision matters.
examples.whyItMatters: A small percentage can be a large pile of product. Precision earns its keep when it changes the cost of being wrong.

examples.title: Danya writes sixty-three on the player card

planSpec.stakes: whether neat tens erase useful differences
planSpec.requiredBeat: she resists rounding because the coach will use the number

examples.scenario: Danya writes 63 on a laminated player card at 10:02 a.m. in the soccer training room, the smell of turf pellets stuck to her shoes. The coach likes numbers ending in zero. They feel honest enough and easier to say. But the winger at 63 percent is not the midfielder at 70, and only one can start on Sunday. Danya caps the marker and leaves the ugly number where it is.
examples.whatToDo: Do not round away a difference the coach will act on. Explain the factors behind 63, then compare it with the other player's risk.
examples.whyItMatters: Neat numbers can make unlike risks look equal. The less pretty number protects the choice from a false tie.

examples.title: Perse audits the number that looked too exact

planSpec.audience: an auditor reviewing a false-precision budget forecast
planSpec.stakes: whether precision came from data or decoration
planSpec.requiredBeat: she traces a decimal back to a guess and changes the rule

examples.scenario: Perse sits at the audit table at 8:49 p.m., calculator tape curling beside a cold falafel wrap. The parks budget forecast had said 14.7 percent overrun. It missed badly. She follows the decimal back through the workbook and finds a guessed permit delay dressed up by a formula. The decimal looked careful because the spreadsheet printed it that way. Perse has to decide what precision rule the next forecast must pass.
examples.whatToDo: Trace each precise number to its source. If a decimal comes from a guess, round it and label the uncertainty instead of letting the sheet look smarter than the evidence.
examples.whyItMatters: False precision borrows trust from arithmetic. Auditing the source keeps numbers honest about what they know and what they are merely guessing.

questions.prompt: A manager at 8:10 a.m. hears a polished forecast for a probability estimate but sees no written odds or date. Which move best fits the skill of using numbers honestly?
choices: Write a dated probability and ask what result would count as a miss.
Trust the confident speaker because clear delivery usually means better judgment.
Wait for perfect proof and refuse to act until uncertainty disappears.

reviewCards.front: You hear a confident claim about a probability estimate. What do you ask before trusting it?
reviewCards.back: Ask for the dated probability, the base rate, and the outcome that would count as a miss. Forecasts improve when they can be checked, not when they sound smooth.

reviewCards.front: A fresh story makes your estimate feel wrong. How should you update?
reviewCards.back: Move the odds by the strength of the new evidence. A vivid story can matter, but it should not erase the older record unless it directly changes the facts.

reviewCards.front: A team wants one bold answer. What smaller move protects learning?
reviewCards.back: Break the issue into dated subquestions. Smaller forecasts show which assumption failed, so the next estimate can improve instead of becoming a blame session.

reviewCards.front: A miss is embarrassing. What should the review preserve?
reviewCards.back: Keep the original wording and number. Then mark which assumption failed. The record has to sting a little or it will not teach.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is using numbers as honest handles for doubt, not as decoration for certainty. Practice means writing the claim before the outcome arrives, then updating it in small, visible steps. The point is not to look cautious. The point is to give reality a way to train you.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a work meeting turns on a probability estimate, then write one dated probability on the agenda and name the result that would prove it wrong.
If you are choosing a health step under uncertainty, then write the base rate you know, the personal fact that changes it, and the next check-in date.
If a personal plan depends on a guess, then split the guess into one small forecast you can check within seven days.
If someone you care about sounds certain about the future, then ask what evidence would make both of you lower the odds by ten points.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before tomorrow night, write one live forecast about a probability estimate with a date, a probability, and two reasons for the number. Put a reminder on the date to check it without rewriting the original line.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review one old forecast before you know the outcome. Move the number only if new evidence deserves it, and write the reason in one sentence.
